strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-motivated gap in RVOS: existing datasets (MeViS, ReVOS, Ref-SAV) do not require reasoning about actor-target roles within an interaction, and the proposed InterRVOS task with paired, role-complementary expressions is a sensible and clearly formalized extension of the task space.

InterRVOS-8K is large-scale (127K expressions, 17,682 actor-target interactions) and the four-stage automatic annotation pipeline is described in detail, including full prompts in the appendix (Figs. A7–A13), which supports reproducibility of the data construction.

The experimental evidence for dataset quality is reasonably convincing: models trained on InterRVOS-5K/2K outperform the much larger Ref-SAV on MeViS both in joint training and zero-shot settings (Table 3), and per-caption-type analysis (Table 4, A1) shows the largest gains on the harder motion-only and multi-instance categories.

The ReVIOSa baseline is a clean, sensible design ([SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens prompting SAM2), and the ablation (Table 6) isolates the benefit of joint actor-target supervision over independent supervision (53.8 -> 59.7), supporting the claim that joint modeling of interaction roles helps.
Additional zero-shot evaluations on Ref-Youtube-VOS and Ref-DAVIS (Table A2) demonstrate that the dataset transfers to standard benchmarks rather than only helping on the authors' own test set.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is never verified by humans. The entire dataset is generated by GPT-4o/LLaMA-70B, yet the paper reports no human audit of expression correctness, mask-expression alignment, or hallucination rates. Visible artifacts (e.g., the ungrammatical 'Person holding for black and brown dog...' in Figure 3) suggest noise, and for a dataset paper this is a material weakness.

The evaluation-set construction is potentially biased: the evaluation videos come from the VidOR training distribution and are filtered toward interaction-centric expressions, and all comparisons in Table 5 are evaluated on this set. It is also unclear whether the compared baselines (Referformer, LMPM, Sa2VA) were fine-tuned on InterRVOS-8K or evaluated zero-shot; if zero-shot, the comparison is unfair, and this is not stated.

The actor-target-aware evaluation protocol is underspecified: how paired expressions are aggregated into a score, how bidirectional vs. unidirectional interactions are scored, and how multi-target cases (e.g., Actor [1] / Target [2], [3] in Figure A2) are handled is not clearly defined.

Some headline claims are weakly supported: ReVIOSa-1B beats Sa2VA-4B by only ~0.5 J&F on the Referring setting (55.8 vs 55.3), and the 4B model underperforms the 1B model on Actor-Target (69.3 vs 69.8) with no discussion of this anomaly.

The architectural contribution is incremental — two additional special tokens plus LoRA tuning on an existing Sa2VA-style SAM2+MLLM stack — so the model side is a baseline rather than a substantive methodological advance, which is acceptable but limits the paper's methodological depth.

Inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine confidence: Section 3 cites VidOR as (Thomee et al., 2016), which is the YFCC100M paper (VidOR is Shang et al., 2019, cited only later); naming shifts between 'InterRVOS', 'InterRVOS', and 'ReVIOSa' across figures and text; there are numerous grammatical errors ('is build upon', 'a actor-target').

Several design details affecting reproducibility are missing, e.g., how mask tracks for multi-object merged expressions are assigned, how the model is trained to decide when to emit both tokens vs. one, and the exact form of the paired-expression supervision during training.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and underexplored gap: existing RVOS benchmarks (Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReVOS, Ref-SAV) do not require models to disentangle actor and target roles within an interaction, and the InterRVOS task formulation with paired complementary expressions is a reasonable way to formalize this gap.

The dataset is claimed to be the largest RVOS-style resource (127K expressions, 8.7K videos) and the comparison in Tables 1-2 is informative; the finding in Table 3 that a 2K-video/28K-expression subset of InterRVOS-8K outperforms the much larger Ref-SAV on MeViS (especially zero-shot: 40.2 vs 32.8) is a genuinely interesting data-efficiency result that supports the value of interaction-centric supervision.

The data annotation pipeline is documented in unusual detail, with the full GPT-4o and LLaMA prompts provided in Appendix A.7-A.13, and implementation details (LoRA on InternVL-2.5, frozen SAM2 encoder, training budget of 4-10 GPU-hours) support reproducibility of the baseline.

The ablation in Table 6 shows a non-trivial gain from jointly generating both [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] masks (53.8 -> 59.7), and the paper appropriately acknowledges that data alone is insufficient for interaction-centric expressions.
The appendix includes dataset statistics (Fig. A3), zero-shot transfer experiments (Table A2), and a limitations section.
weaknesses: No human verification of annotation quality is reported anywhere. The entire dataset is generated by GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B, yet the paper presents no manual audit, no estimated caption-mask agreement rate, and no measure of expression discriminability. For a dataset paper this is a material omission: the visible examples already suggest quality problems (e.g., 'The object moving around the space, handling a metal bowl wrapped in foil... and jeans' conflates a person with an 'object'; 'person handing to person'; the top-50 word frequency is dominated by the generic token 'object'), which would make many expressions ambiguous or ill-posed as referring queries.

The baseline comparisons in Table 5 are questionable: Referformer (2022) and LMPM (2023) are dated and apparently evaluated only zero-shot, while the state-of-the-art claim rests on comparing ReVIOSa to Sa2VA variants on the authors' own automatically generated benchmark. There is no evidence that prior methods were given the opportunity to train on InterRVOS-8K, so 'ReVIOSa achieves state-of-the-art' (Table 5 caption) is not well supported.

The architectural contribution is thin: ReVIOSa is essentially Sa2VA plus two extra special tokens ([SEG_ACT], [SEG_TAR]) that prompt the SAM2 decoder, following the well-established LLaMA+[SEG]+SAM2 recipe. The ablation's 'joint vs. independent' comparison is also confounded: setting (c) receives supervision on both masks simultaneously, so the 5.3-point gain may reflect additional supervision signal rather than the proposed interaction modeling.

There is a train/evaluation contamination concern: the evaluation set is drawn from the VidOR training split, and the training set is also constructed from VidOR. Even if individual videos are disjoint, models evaluated on the benchmark were trained on clips from the identical source distribution with the identical automatic annotation pipeline, which likely inflates absolute numbers relative to how the dataset would transfer to genuinely new domains.

Several factual/presentation errors undermine confidence: the VidOR dataset is cited as (Thomee et al., 2016), which is the YFCC100M paper, not VidOR (Shang et al., 2019); the naming is inconsistent (InterRVOS-8K vs. InterRVOS-2K/5K subsets used in most experiments); Figure 5's 'standard RVOS' prompt examples (Figure A5/A6) reveal that the user prompt explicitly instructs the model to output separate actor/target masks, which weakens claims about emergent actor-target awareness.

The claim that the dataset supports 'temporal dynamics' reasoning is weakly evidenced: the clip extraction (Appendix F) takes only the first 500 frames of the first and last 1,000-frame bins of each video, an arbitrary strategy with no analysis of whether interactions are actually visible or temporally coherent in these clips.

Qualitative comparisons (Fig. 5, A4) are limited to a handful of cherry-picked clips against a single baseline, and the shown masks are sometimes coarse (e.g., 'Adult assisting person' row), providing limited evidence for the broad claims about fine-grained interaction understanding.

strengths: Well-motivated new task: interaction-aware RVOS that requires segmenting both actor and target entities from complementary role-based expressions is a genuine and underexplored extension of standard RVOS, and the paired-expression formulation (actor-focused vs. target-focused views of the same interaction) is a clean and interesting design.

InterRVOS-8K is a substantial resource: 8,738 videos, 35K objects, 127K expressions including 17.6K actor-target interaction expressions, making it the largest RVOS dataset by expression count and the first with explicit actor-target annotations (Tables 1-2).

The four-stage annotation pipeline is described in detail, and the appendix provides the actual prompts used at each stage (Figures A7-A13), which supports transparency and reproducibility of the data construction process.

The core empirical claim about data efficiency is supported: models trained on InterRVOS-2K/5K subsets outperform the much larger Ref-SAV (72K expressions) on MeViS in both joint-training and zero-shot settings (Table 3), and the per-caption-type analysis (Table 4) shows the largest gains on motion-only and multi-instance categories, which is consistent with the dataset's design goals.

The ablation on special tokens (Table 6) isolates the architectural contribution: joint [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] modeling yields +5.3 J&F over a single [SEG] token and +5.3 over independent supervision, giving reasonable evidence that the joint actor-target training signal matters beyond the data.

Useful breadth of experiments: comparisons across training datasets (ReVOS, Ref-SAV, InterRVOS subsets), zero-shot transfer to MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS and Ref-DAVIS (Table A2), and per-type analysis on MeViS valid_u (Table A1), with a sensible proposed actor-target-aware evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: Missing explanation of the provenance of pixel-level segmentation masks. The dataset is built on VidOR (Shang et al., 2019), which provides bounding-box tracklets rather than pixel masks, and the paper (including the appendix) never states how mask tracks for 35,247 objects were obtained. For a dataset paper whose central contribution is annotated masks, this is a material gap that undermines verification of the ground truth.

No human verification or quality audit of the automatically generated annotations. Quality rests entirely on GPT-4o and LLaMA-3.1 outputs; there are no manual inspection statistics, agreement rates, or estimated hallucination rates. Example expressions are often verbose caption-like text ('The object moving around the space, handling a metal bowl wrapped in foil...') rather than discriminative referring expressions, and class-level expressions such as 'person handing to person' or 'Man helping a child' are ambiguous when multiple same-class objects are present, which directly threatens the validity of the J&F evaluation.

The experimental comparisons in Table 5 are not fully specified and may be unfair: it is unclear on what training data the competing methods (Referformer, LMPM, Sa2VA-1B/4B) were trained when evaluated on InterRVOS-8K. Since InterRVOS-8K expressions differ in style and structure from those benchmarks, Sa2VA's lower score could partly reflect distribution mismatch rather than inferior interaction understanding. This weakens the SOTA claim.

The headline claim in Table 3's caption and the text ('Even when controlling the sample size with same expression number') is inconsistent with the table: InterRVOS-2K has 28K expressions versus Ref-SAV's 72K, so expression count is not controlled; only the video count is smaller. The data-efficiency argument remains plausible but is overstated as written.

The architecture contribution is modest: ReVIOSa is essentially Sa2VA (InternVL-2.5 + SAM2 + LoRA) plus two additional special tokens and a corresponding supervision scheme. The dataset, not the method, carries the paper, yet Table 4 shows interaction-category performance with the baseline architecture trained on InterRVOS-5K (60.6) is actually slightly below training on MeViS (61.6), and the gains from ReVIOSa on the interaction category (+5.1) are the smallest among categories, suggesting the interaction modeling problem is far from solved by the proposed baseline.

Some framing is overstated: the claim that prior datasets focus 'solely on actor-only' settings ignores that A2D-Sentences expressions routinely reference interacting objects (e.g., 'a person lifting weights', 'a person riding a bicycle'); the genuine novelty is segmenting the target in addition to the actor, which should be stated more carefully.

Presentation issues that should be corrected: the citation 'VidOR (Thomee et al., 2016)' is wrong (Thomee et al. 2016 is YFCC100M; VidOR is Shang et al. 2019); the project page URL is left blank ('available at:'); the naming 'InterRVOS-8K' alongside '127K samples' is confusing; Figure 1's premise about existing datasets is partly inaccurate; minor grammatical errors appear throughout (e.g., 'is build upon', 'a action-target').

Evaluation set construction details are thin: the filtering process used to increase the proportion of interaction-centric expressions is not specified, and it is unclear how the actor-target pairing in the new evaluation protocol interacts with mask-assignment ambiguity for multi-object targets (e.g., Actor [1] / Target [2],[3]).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated task formulation: InterRVOS extends RVOS by requiring separate segmentation of actor and target objects within interaction expressions, addressing a genuine gap (role asymmetry) that prior RVOS work (MeViS, ReVOS, Ref-SAV) does not capture.

Substantial dataset contribution: InterRVOS-127K (127K expressions, 8.7K videos) is the largest RVOS-style dataset with explicit actor-target mask annotations; the four-stage automatic annotation pipeline is documented in detail (Appendix D, including full prompts), and the evaluation split (738 videos) was human-refined.

Comprehensive architecture evaluation: ablations isolate the contributions of interaction-aware special tokens (+2.6 J&F) and attention mask loss (+1.5 J&F), and the layer-head selection strategy for AML is supported by attention-magnitude analysis (Figures 6, A1, A2) and motivation experiments linking attention concentration to segmentation quality.

Useful evidence beyond the self-proposed benchmark: dataset ablations (Tables A2, A3) show models trained on InterRVOS subsets outperform Ref-SAV-trained models on MeViS in both joint-training and zero-shot settings, suggesting the interaction-centric supervision is genuinely more informative rather than merely in-domain; competitive standard-benchmark results (MeViS 49.3 with a 4B model vs. Sa2VA-4B 46.2).

Detailed appendix supporting reproducibility: implementation details (InternVL-2.5 + LoRA, SAM2 decoder fine-tuning, training hours/hardware), annotation prompts, dataset statistics, and additional qualitative results are provided.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is unclear on the headline table: Table 2 evaluates existing baselines (Referformer, LMPM, VISA, VideoLISA, Sa2VA) on InterRVOS-127K, but the paper does not specify whether these baselines were retrained on the new dataset, fine-tuned, or evaluated zero-shot/adapted. Since ReVIOSa is trained on this exact data while the baselines were designed for actor-only segmentation, the claim of state-of-the-art on InterRVOS-127K risks conflating dataset advantage, architecture advantage, and training advantage. A controlled comparison (e.g., Sa2VA-style baseline with two [SEG] tokens trained identically) is partially covered by ablation (i)-(iv) but only with their own backbone.

Annotation quality of the training data is not quantitatively validated. Only the evaluation set (738 videos) was human-refined; there is no reported human audit of the 122K automatically generated training expressions/masks (e.g., hallucination rate of GPT-4o/LLaMA captions, actor-target assignment accuracy, mask-track correctness from SAM2). Given the entire task hinges on correct role assignment, this is a material gap.

AML, while empirically effective, is a heuristic technique: the layer-head selection (top-1 layer by attention magnitude, top-4 heads) is validated only empirically on this specific model scale/dataset, and the choice of binary cross-entropy on resized patch-level masks is not analyzed against alternatives. Generalization of the selection protocol across models/backbones is only briefly addressed (1B vs 4B).

Claims on standard RVOS benchmarks are mixed rather than uniformly state-of-the-art: ReVIOSa-4B beats Sa2VA on MeViS (49.3 vs 46.2) but trails on Ref-DAVIS (71.6 vs 73.8); the paper's blanket SOTA framing should be tempered.

No role-confusion or error analysis for the core novel capability: the paper reports aggregate J&F for actor and target but does not measure how often the model swaps actor/target roles, nor performance breakdown by interaction type (unidirectional vs. bidirectional) or by number of involved objects, which would directly validate the claimed role-awareness.

Presentation issues: several grammar/typo problems ('it's' for possessives in Figure A6, 'an single object', incomplete sentence in Related Work 'even when interaction expressions involving distinct actor and target roles inherently'), the project-page URL is blank in the abstract, and Figure 1's actor/target examples could be more precisely explained. These are correctable but reflect insufficient polish.

Potential domain bias: the dataset is built solely on VidOR (household/user-generated video), so conclusions about interaction modeling may not transfer to other video domains; the paper does not discuss this limitation.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap in RVOS: existing formulations segment only the actor even when expressions describe directional interactions, and the proposed InterRVOS task (separate actor/target segmentation with a role-aware evaluation protocol) is a reasonable and clearly motivated extension of the task space.

InterRVOS-127K is a substantial resource: 127K automatically annotated expressions on 8.7K video clips with distinct actor/target mask tracks, and the annotation pipeline is documented in detail (Appendix D.1, full GPT-4o/LLaMA prompts in Figures A12-A18), which supports reproducibility.

The evaluation set was human-refined (expressions and masks), and useful dataset analyses are provided (statistics in Fig. A8, word frequency, interaction distributions, clip extraction procedure in D.3).

The ablation study (Table 4) cleanly separates the contributions of the interaction-aware special tokens (+2.6 J&F) and the attention mask loss (+1.5 J&F), and the layer-head selection analysis (Figs. 6-7, A1-A2) is thorough, including a correlation analysis motivating AML (Fig. A1).

The dataset demonstrates value beyond the new task: Tables A2-A3 show that models trained on InterRVOS subsets outperform Ref-SAV training on MeViS in both joint-training and zero-shot settings with fewer samples, and ReVIOSa-4B achieves competitive zero-shot results (e.g., 49.3 on MeViS vs. 46.2 for Sa2VA-4B).
weaknesses: Baseline comparison fairness is unclear and likely favorable to the authors. Table 2 does not state whether competing methods (Referformer, LMPM, VISA, VideoLISA, Sa2VA) were trained on InterRVOS-127K or evaluated zero-shot. If zero-shot, the InterRVOS-Actor/RVOS comparisons are not meaningful since ReVIOSa was trained on in-domain data. This ambiguity undermines the central empirical claim of state-of-the-art performance.

No meaningful baseline exists for the InterRVOS-Target setting. The '-' entries for all prior methods are expected since they were never designed for this, but the authors could have adapted a strong baseline (e.g., running Sa2VA twice with role-swapped prompts, which their own dataset conveniently provides as paired expressions) to establish whether the task requires their architecture. Without this, the necessity of ReVIOSa's design is not established.

The methodological novelty is incremental: two extra [SEG] tokens plus a BCE loss on attention maps are simple extensions of the standard LISA/Sa2VA-style recipe, and supervising attention maps with masks has precedent in the attention-guidance literature. The layer-head selection strategy (top-1 layer, top-4 heads) is purely empirical and architecture-specific, raising generalization concerns.

Data quality of the training split is not verified: only the 5,048-expression evaluation set was human-corrected, while the 122K training expressions and SAM2-derived masks from VidOR are fully automatic. No annotation quality metrics (e.g., sampled human verification rates, mask IoU against ground truth, expression hallucination rate) are reported, which is a significant omission for a dataset paper.

Several causal/interpretive claims are under-supported, e.g., 'the surpassing performance on InterRVOS-Actor indicates that explicitly segmenting both the actor and the target enhances the model's ability to localize the actor itself' is a correlation-based inference without a controlled experiment.

The paper's writing has recurring grammatical and incomplete-sentence issues (e.g., 'even when interaction expressions involving distinct actor and target roles inherently', 'assesses segmentation performance separately for actor and target separately', 'which the brief concept illustrated in Figure 4'), which detracts from clarity.

On standard benchmarks the gains are mixed: ReVIOSa-4B trails Sa2VA-4B on Ref-DAVIS (71.6 vs. 73.8) and only marginally leads on Ref-Youtube-VOS (70.5 vs. 70.0), so the claim of strong standard-RVOS performance is qualified.

The RVOS-setting rows in Table 2 conflate differences in training data and architecture across methods, making it difficult to attribute gains to interaction modeling rather than to data volume or the MLLM backbone.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined new task: InterRVOS extends standard RVOS by requiring separate segmentation of actor and target objects under directional interaction expressions, filling a genuine gap since existing RVOS methods (MeViS, ReVOS, Ref-SAV lineage) segment only the actor.

Substantial dataset contribution: InterRVOS-127K is the largest RVOS dataset to date (127K expressions, 8.7K videos, 17.6K actor-target interaction expressions) and, per Table 1/A4, the first with distinct actor/target mask annotations. The stage-wise annotation pipeline is documented in detail, including complete GPT-4o and LLaMA prompts (Figures A12-A18), which supports reproducibility.

Evidence for dataset quality beyond self-evaluation: Tables A2 and A3 show models trained on subsets of InterRVOS-127K (28K/71K expressions) outperform training on Ref-SAV (72K) on MeViS in both joint-training and zero-shot settings, which is a fair, controlled comparison supporting the claim of superior supervision quality.

Ablations support each architectural component: Table 4 shows special tokens (+2.6 J&F) and AML (+1.5 J&F) each improve over baseline and combine complementarily; Figures 6-7 and Appendix B provide a principled, empirically validated layer-head selection strategy for AML, and Figure A1 motivates AML via correlation between attention concentration in mask regions and segmentation quality.

Competitive generalization to standard RVOS: ReVIOSa-4B (49.3 MeViS, 70.5 Ref-YouTube-VOS, 71.6 Ref-DAVIS) outperforms VISA-13B and is comparable to Sa2VA-4B despite a smaller base model, indicating the interaction-aware training is not overfit to the new task.
Extensive appendix: implementation details, training cost, per-model-scale analyses, qualitative comparisons, and dataset statistics are thorough, exceeding typical reporting standards.
weaknesses: The headline results (Table 2) are evaluated on the authors' own benchmark, where no baseline is applicable to the InterRVOS-Target setting; the target-segmentation numbers (67-68 J&F) cannot be compared against any external method, so the SOTA claim on the new task is inherently self-referential. Only the InterRVOS-Actor and standard-RVOS columns permit external comparison.

Training annotations are fully automatic (SAM2 mask tracks + GPT-4o/LLaMA captions) and only the small evaluation set (738 videos) was human-refined. No annotation quality metrics (e.g., human verification rate of train expressions, actor/target role accuracy, mask IoU against human labels on a train subsample) are reported, so the reliability of the 122K training expressions is unquantified.

Actor/target supervision ultimately derives from VidOR tracked object identities propagated through SAM2; role assignment correctness depends on GPT-4o judgments over highlighted frames, and systematic errors here (e.g., directionality confusion) would be invisible in the standard J&F metrics used.

The model decides at inference whether an expression involves an interaction and thus whether to emit [SEG_TAR]; no quantitative analysis of this binary decision's accuracy (false positives/negatives) is provided, which is central to the task.

The layer-head selection for AML (top-1 layer, top-4 heads) is empirical and model-specific (L22/H05,H07,H10,H11 for 1B; L33/H13,H12,H14,H06 for 4B), and Table 3 shows non-monotonic sensitivity (k=3 drops to 60.5 while k=4 gives 62.0), raising concerns about hyperparameter brittleness and whether the recipe transfers to other MLLMs.

Architecture novelty is moderate: the method is a natural extension of the established [SEG]-token LISA/Sa2VA paradigm (splitting one token into two, plus attention supervision on self-attention maps, which has precedents in attention-guided grounding). The contribution leans more on the task/dataset than the modeling.

Interactions are restricted to VidOR-derived clips (heavily person-centric, ≤500-frame clips, first/last 1K-frame bins only), which may limit interaction type diversity; ~35% of videos contain no interaction expression, and only actor-target pairs/triples are covered.

Several baselines in Table 2 (Referformer, LMPM, VISA) are considerably older/weaker than the modern MLLM baselines; it is also not fully clear how non-MLLM baselines were trained/evaluated on InterRVOS-127K. Minor but noticeable writing and grammatical issues (e.g., 'which the brief concept illustrated in Figure 4', 'role-aware segmentation under interaction-aware expressions' phrasing) require polishing.
